data.title: Dollarama Earnings Call: Strong Growth Amid Global Headwinds
data.description:
Dollarama ((TSE:DOL)) has held its Q2 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Dollarama struck an upbeat tone on its latest earnings call, with management emphasizing strong second‑quarter results, healthy traffic trends and expanding store networks at home and abroad. Executives acknowledged macroeconomic and cost headwinds, but insisted that the discount chain’s value proposition and disciplined cost control leave it well positioned to navigate a cautious consumer backdrop.

Strong Consolidated Revenue and Earnings Growth

Consolidated sales jumped 17.6% to more than $2 billion in Q2 fiscal 2027, underpinned by solid demand across key categories and geographies. EBITDA rose 11% to $653 million, delivering a robust 32.2% margin, while net earnings reached $349.3 million and diluted EPS climbed 11.2% to $1.29 from $1.16 a year earlier.

Promotion

70% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

Canadian Same-Store Sales and Traffic Momentum

In Canada, same‑store sales advanced 5.4%, outpacing last year’s 4.9% growth and reflecting sustained customer engagement. Traffic increased 3.7%, following 3.5% growth in Q1, with basket growth and steady seasonal performance, including positive summer sales, reinforcing Dollarama’s appeal to value‑seeking shoppers.

Raised Canadian Same-Store Sales Guidance

On the back of a strong first half, management lifted fiscal 2027 Canadian same‑store sales guidance to a range of 4% to 4.5%, up from 3% to 4%. The company framed the new outlook as confident but prudent, balancing momentum seen year‑to‑date with an acknowledgement that macro uncertainty could temper spending later in the year.

Expanded Canadian Store Network

Dollarama continued to build out its domestic footprint, opening 15 net new stores in Q2 and 43 year‑to‑date, taking its Canadian network to roughly 1,730 locations. Reflecting the accelerated pace, fiscal 2027 guidance for net new Canadian stores was raised to between 65 and 75, from a prior target of 60 to 70.

Western Canada Logistics Hub Progress

Construction of a new Western Canada logistics hub is advancing on schedule, with full operation expected by the end of calendar 2027. The facility will support a two‑node distribution model in Canada, aiming to improve efficiency, reduce transportation costs and support continued store growth across the network.

Dollarcity Store Growth and Earnings Contribution

Dollarama’s Dollarcity venture in Central and South America remained a key growth engine, adding 19 net new stores in Q2 for a total of about 6,760 locations. Dollarama’s share of Dollarcity net earnings rose 30.3% to CAD 49.9 million, including a 39.7% year‑over‑year increase from its 60% stake across the four regional markets.

Dollarcity Dividend Declared

Following quarter end, Dollarcity declared a US$125 million cash dividend, its second of the fiscal year, underscoring confidence in its cash generation. Dollarama will receive US$75.1 million, adding to its own financial flexibility and supporting a broader capital allocation strategy focused on shareholder returns.

Mexico Expansion Remains on Plan

The company’s push into Mexico is gathering pace, with 10 new stores opened in Q2, taking the network from 11 to 21 locations by quarter end. Management said the ramp‑up is proceeding as planned, density is building in the Guadalajara region, and initial customer response to Dollarama’s value and convenience offering has been encouraging.

Australia Store Transformation Accelerated

In Australia, Dollarama accelerated its store transformation roadmap, renovating 25 locations during Q2, up from 13 in Q1, and opening four net new stores. At midyear, 60 stores featured the Dollarama layout and fixtures, more than doubling from 28 at the end of Q1, within a national fleet of 414 outlets.

Australia Transformation Targets Remain on Track

Despite near‑term earnings pressure, management reiterated that Australian transformation targets for fiscal 2027 remain intact. The plan is to renovate between 60 and 80 stores and open between 15 and 25 net new locations, reshaping the chain’s merchandising and price architecture for longer‑term growth.

Australian Import Assortment Rollout Began

The first wave of Dollarama‑sourced import products hit Australian shelves during Q2, marking an important step in aligning assortments. The company aims to have roughly half of import products transitioned by fiscal year‑end, with the gradual rollout and assortment work continuing into fiscal 2028.

Canadian Gross Margin and Expense Guidance Maintained

Canadian gross margin held at 45.7% of sales in Q2 versus 45.6% a year ago, aided by the benefits of scale and a tight handle on sourcing. SG&A expenses were 13.8% of sales, roughly flat year over year, and management kept full‑year guidance for gross margin at 45.0% to 45.5% and SG&A at 14.1% to 14.6%.

Capital Returned to Shareholders

Dollarama continued to deploy capital to shareholders, repurchasing more than 1.5 million common shares for cancellation during the quarter at a cost of $300.4 million. The board also signed off on a quarterly cash dividend of 12¢ per share, reflecting confidence in recurring cash flows.

Strong Toy Category Performance

Management highlighted toys as a standout performer, delivering significantly better results than historically seen during the quarter. Most other categories remained in line with recent trends, suggesting broad stability in consumer demand across Dollarama’s merchandise mix.

Value Proposition Continues to Resonate

Executives stressed that customers increasingly rely on Dollarama for dependable value as household budgets come under strain and confidence remains subdued. Fixed price points, careful assortment management, dense store locations and a consistent shopping experience were cited as pillars of the chain’s ongoing relevance.

No Additional Price Point Currently Needed

Despite inflation pressures in the broader economy, management said there is currently no need to add a new price tier above the $5 maximum. Any higher price point would only be considered if cost inflation reached a level that made the existing cap unsustainable over time.

Consumer and Macroeconomic Pressure

The company nonetheless described Canadian economic conditions as challenging, with cautious consumers and elevated living costs weighing on spending. Weak confidence, trade tensions and broader uncertainty are all seen as factors that could restrain the pace of growth, even for a discount‑focused retailer.

Higher Oil and Supply Chain Costs Expected to Intensify

Management warned that higher oil prices are pushing up raw material and transportation costs, with more impact likely ahead. While supply chain pressures were managed effectively in Q2, the lag before these costs flow through the income statement means they are expected to become more visible starting in Q3.

Tariff and Geopolitical Exposure

Dollarama faces direct tariff exposure through Canadian counter tariffs on certain goods imported from the United States, though the impact is currently described as manageable. Geopolitical conflicts are also creating broader cost pressures across global supply chains, but Q2 tariff effects were largely mitigated.

Potential Further Cost Escalation Could Affect Outlook

Management said it is comfortable maintaining current Canadian gross margin guidance as long as cost conditions remain relatively stable. However, a further escalation in input costs or a sustained period of elevated pressures could force a reassessment of the margin outlook later on.

Australia Sales Pressure from Merchandise Transition

In Australia, the ongoing shift to lower‑priced merchandise is expected to continue weighing on sales throughout fiscal 2027. The impact should be more pronounced in the second half as the transition pace accelerates, with management framing the change as a near‑term rebasing to reset the mix and price‑point structure.

Australian Operating Losses and Second-Half Costs

The Australian business was running at an operating loss of roughly $25 million at the fiscal‑year midpoint, reflecting integration and transformation spending. Those costs are expected to be more heavily weighted toward the second half, implying a step‑up in Q3, which is also a seasonally weaker period for that market.

Australian Product Transition Still at an Early Stage

The rollout of Dollarama‑sourced products in Australia is still in its infancy, leaving limited data on how shoppers are reacting. Management said a denser assortment is needed before it can draw conclusions, and reiterated that the product transition will remain gradual and carefully controlled.

Mexico Ramp-Up Losses

The Mexican expansion is generating start‑up losses, with Dollarama booking a CAD 5.7 million loss tied to its 80% stake in the ramp‑up. Management stressed that these losses are in line with expectations for a new market and are not altering long‑term confidence in the opportunity.

Earthquake Temporarily Affected Colombian Stores

An earthquake in Colombia after quarter end temporarily disrupted operations at a limited number of Dollarcity stores, adding a short‑term complication. The company said activity has largely normalized and the expected financial impact from the event should be minimal.

Dollarcity Growth Rates Expected to Moderate Over Time

Executives cautioned investors against extrapolating Dollarcity’s current high growth rates indefinitely, noting that 40% to 50% annual expansion is not sustainable forever. As the chain’s base becomes larger, management expects percentage growth to naturally moderate even if the franchise remains a key driver.

Operating Costs Growing Faster Than Inflation in Some Areas

Certain SG&A line items, including spending tied to recycling initiatives, are rising faster than inflation, squeezing operating leverage. Management said its objective is to hold SG&A as a percentage of sales steady while also controlling cost of goods sold, a balancing act that will require ongoing discipline.

Prudent Second-Half Same-Store Sales Outlook

While first‑half momentum justified a higher full‑year same‑store sales target, Dollarama emphasized that its outlook for the second half remains cautious. The company pointed to higher oil prices, trade headlines, continued household budget pressure and macro uncertainties as potential drags on sentiment and spending.

Guidance and Outlook

Dollarama now expects to add 65 to 75 net new stores in Canada this fiscal year and deliver same‑store sales growth of 4% to 4.5%, while maintaining gross margin and SG&A guidance for the Canadian segment. In Australia, the group remains on track to renovate 60 to 80 stores, open 15 to 25 new locations and transition about half of import products by year‑end, with integration costs weighted to the seasonally weak second half.

Dollarama’s earnings call painted the picture of a value retailer in expansion mode, balancing strong financial performance with disciplined caution about external risks. For investors, the story is one of solid Canadian execution, promising growth in Latin America and early‑stage bets in Mexico and Australia that may pressure profits now but could underpin longer‑term upside.

data.title: Nike Inc. Earnings Call: Performance Strength, China Drag
data.description:
Nike Inc ((NKE)) has held its Q1 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Nike Inc.’s latest earnings call struck a cautious tone, balancing solid operational progress in its Performance portfolio against clear near-term financial pressure. Management highlighted innovation, margin improvement and strong cash generation, but acknowledged that revenue declines in Sportswear, Jordan and Greater China, along with a multi-year reset, will weigh on results before any full turnaround takes hold.

Q1 Results Met Guidance but Revenue Fell

Nike said first-quarter results landed squarely within its earlier guidance, with revenue, gross margin and costs tracking expectations. Even so, quarterly revenue declined 4% to $11.2 billion, or 5% on a currency-neutral basis, and earnings per share dipped 2% year over year to $0.48, underscoring that the business remains in transition.

Promotion

70% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

Performance Portfolio Shows Broad-Based Strength

The Performance portfolio continued to be the bright spot, growing high single digits in Q1 and building toward a $16 billion business by fiscal 2026. Growth was broad-based across Running, Global Football, Training, Basketball, Tennis and Golf, signaling that Nike’s competitive position in core sports remains solid despite macro and category headwinds.

Running Continues to Gain Market Share

Running delivered another quarter of double-digit growth with consistent share gains across key categories. Nike noted it has nearly tripled its share of the Max cushioning segment over the past year, powered by the Vomero franchise, and it launched four new running footwear innovations in the past two months to keep momentum intact.

Global Football Benefits from World Cup Tailwinds

Global Football posted strong double-digit growth across all four geographies, boosted by heightened World Cup enthusiasm. World Cup team-kit sales doubled compared with the 2022 tournament, while club football kits grew in the high teens, highlighting the brand’s ability to capitalize on major global events.

Training, Tennis, Golf and Basketball Extend Growth

Beyond Running and Football, Nike saw global growth in Training, led by EMEA, with Tennis and Golf both posting double-digit gains. Basketball delivered double-digit growth in North America, supported by new concepts such as the Hybrid Footwear System for running and strength movements and the Hyperslide recovery product.

Women’s Basketball Expansion Accelerates

Nike highlighted explosive growth in its women’s signature basketball business, which has expanded nearly 500% from fiscal 2022 to fiscal 2026. The Caitlin 1 became Nike Basketball’s largest women’s signature launch ever, debuting in 5,000 retail doors, roughly double the typical footprint for a Nike Basketball signature shoe.

North America Performance Drives Modest Growth

In North America, revenue grew 2%, supported by strength in Running, Global Football and Basketball. The company reported healthy sell-through of performance products across sporting-goods retailers, specialty accounts and other distribution channels, a sign that demand for core sport offerings remains resilient.

Islands of Strength Within Sportswear

Although overall Sportswear revenue declined, Nike pointed to several bright spots within the category. The Air Force 1 supported a stable full-price business, Running-inspired franchises such as the P-6000 and V5 Runner grew strong double digits, and Studio Fleece emerged as Nike Inc.’s best-performing apparel collection of the quarter.

Running and Flagship Retail Momentum in China

China remains challenged, but the Running category delivered double-digit growth for the sixth consecutive quarter, suggesting the brand still resonates with performance consumers. The China After Dark Tour attracted nearly 4,000 runners and sold out on its first day, while the Shanghai House of Innovation posted 10 straight months of growth, offering pockets of optimism.

Gross Margin Improvement and Cost Discipline

Nike’s margin and cost actions are beginning to show results, with first-quarter gross margin rising 60 basis points year over year to 42.8%. The improvement was driven by supply-chain cost management and foreign-exchange tailwinds, while SG&A declined 3% even as the company stepped up demand-creation spending tied to the World Cup.

Balance Sheet Remains a Strategic Asset

The company ended the quarter with $8.4 billion in cash and short-term investments and remained in a net cash position, with leverage around 2x. Nike returned approximately $610 million to shareholders through dividends and reiterated that the dividend remains a key capital-allocation priority despite the near-term earnings pressure.

Pace Program Targets Productivity and Speed

Central to Nike’s long-term plan is the Pace program, aimed at improving speed to market and sharpening operational focus. The initiative seeks to streamline decision-making, evolve the supply chain, move resources closer to key countries and consumers, and ultimately deliver about $2.5 billion in savings, with the largest benefits expected at the end of the decade.

Investing in Supply Chain and Operating Model

Nike is backing its productivity push with structural changes, including a new capability-focused campus in Bengaluru, India. The company plans to reorganize into three geographies and continue investing in product creation and marketplace capabilities, with teams expected to transition to the new geographic formation in fiscal 2028.

Localized Consumer Engagement and Partnerships

On the demand side, Nike is leaning into local activations and partnerships to deepen consumer engagement, citing a recent Austin event around the Texas-Ohio State football game. That activation brought together Running, Training, Football and Sportswear, featured Texas-specific fleece collections, and was supported by 13 new NIL athlete partnerships spanning eight sports.

Revenue Decline Highlights Transitional Phase

Despite operational wins, overall revenue weakness underlined the challenges ahead, with Q1 revenue falling to $11.2 billion. Earnings per share decreased modestly, reflecting a business that is still navigating portfolio resets and category-specific headwinds as management works to realign supply and demand.

Sportswear Weakness Weighs Heavily on Results

Sportswear, which accounted for just under half of quarterly revenue, declined in the low double digits as Nike deliberately pulled back in certain areas. Management cited product underperformance and broader marketplace pressure, signaling that the lifestyle side of the business is undergoing a necessary but painful reset.

Dunk Pullback and Inventory Cleanup Hurt Near Term

A planned reduction in Dunk revenue weighed materially on results, with the category down nearly 50% and creating about a $200 million headwind in Sportswear. Nike also noted that some aged, high-volume Sportswear footwear sold below expectations, forcing adjustments to future wholesale orders as it works with partners to clear excess inventory.

Lifestyle Market Lacks Energy

Nike emphasized that a lack of “energy” in the lifestyle marketplace is dampening traffic, while consumers remain cautious. In response, the company aims to bring more creativity to Sportswear and is restructuring assortments around distinct consumer needs and style preferences to reignite demand.

Jordan Brand Hit by Oversupply of Retros

Jordan Brand, which represented 13% of Nike’s global business in Q1, saw revenue fall by the mid-teens. Management admitted it oversupplied iconic retro products and plans to reduce the volume and frequency of certain Retro launches, with North America expected to bear the brunt of the near-term impact as the brand recalibrates.

Greater China Sees Sharp Decline

Greater China revenue dropped 26% in Q1 as Nike pushed ahead with a significant marketplace reset, including eliminating unprofitable or brand-dilutive online distribution. The company is reducing digital storefronts, refreshing physical retail and improving inventories, but warned that revenue and profitability will stay under pressure for multiple seasons.

China Outlook to Worsen Before It Improves

Management said its fiscal 2027 outlook assumes that Greater China revenue will deteriorate further for the balance of the year as reset actions continue. The company cautioned that pressure from China could extend into fiscal 2028, making the region a key swing factor in Nike’s medium-term growth trajectory.

Mixed Trends Across Other Geographies

Outside China, Nike’s results were uneven, with EMEA revenue down 5% in Q1 and APLA flat. These declines were partially offset by the 2% growth in North America, underscoring that performance-centric strength in the U.S. cannot yet fully offset pockets of weakness in other regions.

Performance Not Yet Large Enough to Offset Drag

Nike acknowledged that its growing Performance business is still too small to counterbalance the drag from Sportswear, Jordan and Greater China. Sportswear and Jordan together represented a high single-digit drag on consolidated Nike, and management noted that excluding the Greater China reset, Performance would have grown low double digits.

Guidance Signals High Single-Digit Revenue Decline

Looking ahead to fiscal 2027, Nike currently expects revenues to decline in the high single-digit range, with deliberate supply reductions and portfolio actions pressuring reported sales into fiscal 2028. The company also expects profitability to fall more than revenue, as gross-margin pressure, fixed-cost deleverage and higher input costs outweigh savings from disciplined expense management.

Pace Savings Offset by Near-Term Implementation Costs

Fiscal 2027 adjusted earnings per share is projected in a range of $1.15 to $1.35, excluding impact from the Pace program. Pace is expected to deliver about $2.5 billion in savings, but comes with roughly $1 billion in implementation costs plus $300 million of severance-related charges, with most savings realized in fiscal 2029 and 2030 and full impact continuing into fiscal 2031.

Business Still Below Long-Term Potential

Management was frank that recent financial results have fallen short of expectations and remain below Nike’s long-term potential. Considerable work lies ahead to restore Sportswear, Jordan, Converse and Greater China to financial health, but the company views its strong Performance engine, cash position and productivity program as foundations for eventual recovery.

In summary, Nike’s earnings call painted a picture of a global brand in the midst of a deliberate reset, with strong performance categories offset by lifestyle and regional pressures. Investors will be watching closely to see whether the Pace program, portfolio pruning and innovation pipeline can bridge the gap between near-term declines and the company’s ambitious long-term targets.

data.title: MHP SE Earnings Call: Growth Offsets Mounting Strain
data.description:
MHP SE Sponsored GDR RegS ((GB:MHPC)) has held its Q2 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

MHP SE’s latest earnings call painted a picture of a company balancing solid operational progress with mounting financial strain. Management highlighted strong revenue growth, stable first-half adjusted EBITDA and rapid expansion in Europe and vegetable oils. Yet these gains were offset by a $57 million net loss, margin compression, fragile poultry economics and persistent disruptions in Ukraine’s logistics and infrastructure.

Revenue Surges on UVESA Consolidation

Revenue for the first six months of 2026 rose 32% year-on-year to about $2.161 billion. The main driver was the consolidation of Spanish poultry group UVESA within the European operating segment, which materially boosted top-line scale and regional diversification.

Promotion

70% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

EBITDA Holds Steady Despite Poultry Weakness

Adjusted EBITDA, net of IFRS 16, was broadly stable at $232 million compared with $236 million in the first half of 2025. This resilience came even as poultry profitability deteriorated sharply, underscoring the cushioning effect of other segments and geographies.

Second Quarter Shows Sequential Operating Rebound

Management reported a meaningful sequential improvement in the second quarter, particularly in poultry. Poultry adjusted EBITDA climbed 58% quarter-on-quarter as pricing stabilized, suggesting that the worst of the immediate pressure may have passed.

Agriculture EBITDA More Than Doubles

Agricultural revenue was roughly flat year-on-year at $186 million for the first six months. However, gross profit and adjusted EBITDA more than doubled, driven by significantly improved market prices for grains and oilseeds in June and July that briefly lifted margins.

European Segment Delivers Strong Growth

The European operating segment’s revenue more than doubled year-on-year to $738 million in the first half, fueled by UVESA consolidation and higher processed meat volumes and prices. Gross profit jumped 57% to $124 million, while EBITDA surged 76% to $86 million, making Europe a key profit engine.

European Results Strengthen in Q2

In the second quarter alone, European segment revenue more than doubled year-on-year and rose 8% quarter-on-quarter to $384 million. Gross profit increased 26% year-on-year to $59 million and EBITDA climbed 47% to $44 million, confirming momentum in the region.

Poultry Revenues Rise Amid Pricing Pressure

Poultry and related operations revenue increased 10% year-on-year and 15% quarter-on-quarter to $523 million in Q2, with six-month revenue up 9% to $976 million. Growth was driven by higher byproduct sales and energy products such as biomethane, partly offsetting weaker core meat pricing.

Value-Added Poultry and Processed Meats Grow

Both poultry meat and processed meat volumes grew year-on-year and quarter-on-quarter. Processed meat volumes benefited from a continued shift toward higher value-added products, and pricing for these offerings remained on an upward trend, supporting mix and margins.

Vegetable Oils Expand Rapidly

Vegetable oil revenue jumped 38% year-on-year and 25% quarter-on-quarter to $145 million in Q2, with six-month revenue up 17% to $261 million. Higher sunflower and soybean oil prices and increased sunflower oil volumes were key contributors to the segment’s expansion.

New Sunflower Line Boosts Capacity

A newly launched sunflower extraction line significantly increased oil yield and processing capacity. Sunflower oil production doubled from about 25,000 tonnes per month last year to around 50,000 tonnes, with utilization reportedly near 100%, improving operating leverage.

Vegetable Oil Profitability Improves

Vegetable oil gross profit rose in both the second quarter and first half, driven by higher sales volumes and better sunflower oil margins. Adjusted EBITDA reached $7 million in Q2 and $10 million for the first six months, turning the segment into a growing earnings contributor.

Crop Yields Remain Resilient

Winter crops delivered solid results, with wheat yields at 6.7 tonnes per hectare and rapeseed at 3.8 tonnes per hectare. Spring crop yields are expected to be broadly in line with last year, supporting supply security despite the challenging Ukrainian backdrop.

Export Routes Adapted After Port Attacks

Following attacks on Black Sea port infrastructure, MHP adjusted poultry export routes without major impact on EU and U.K. volumes. Shipments to MENA and South Africa were rerouted via Klaipeda and Constanta, while about half of vegetable oil exports went directly through Ukraine’s western border into Europe.

European Expansion Progresses

Perutnina Ptuj continued to show solid operational performance, while UVESA’s integration is proceeding as planned. Management said it already sees improvements in UVESA’s operational efficiency, reinforcing the strategic rationale for the acquisition.

Payán Deal Strengthens Spanish Foothold

On June 16, 2026, UVESA acquired 100% of Spanish poultry company Payán for EUR 28 million, generating EUR 17 million of goodwill. The transaction was described as strengthening MHP’s position in the Spanish poultry market and deepening its European base.

Liquidity and Covenants Remain Solid

Cash and cash equivalents stood at $348 million at mid-year, providing a liquidity cushion. The group remained in full compliance with bank covenants, with an acquisition leverage ratio of 2.8:1 on a pro forma basis, comfortably below the 3.0 threshold.

Refinancing Pushes Out Debt Maturities

MHP refinanced $550 million of Senior Notes due 2026 with new Senior Notes maturing in 2029. This refinancing shifted the debt profile toward longer-term obligations, partially easing near-term refinancing pressure.

Investments Support Energy Resilience

Management emphasized that the company is well positioned to handle energy disruptions. This is attributed to a long-term capital expenditure program started in 2022, aimed at bolstering energy resilience across operations.

Ukraine’s Macro Environment Remains Strained

The Ukrainian operating backdrop remains difficult, with continued missile attacks, infrastructure damage and pressure on the energy system. The National Bank of Ukraine expects full-year GDP growth of around 2%, highlighting a fragile recovery.

Currency Weakness and Inflation Persist

The hryvnia weakened to roughly UAH 44.5 per U.S. dollar, while average annual inflation is expected at 9.4%. Quarter-on-quarter CPI eased to about 2.2% in Q2 from 3.4% in Q1, providing slight relief but still weighing on costs and purchasing power.

Mixed Grain and Sunflower Harvest Trends

Sunflower production declined 7% year-on-year to around 10 million tonnes nationally. In contrast, total grain output rose 13% to approximately 63.5 million tonnes, supporting the broader agricultural supply picture.

Group Profitability Under Pressure

Despite 32% revenue growth, gross profit rose only 8% to $397 million. Operating profit fell 17% year-on-year, EBITDA margin dropped from 14% to 11%, and the group posted a $57 million net loss, partly due to a $75 million foreign exchange loss versus a gain last year.

Poultry Profitability Deteriorates Sharply

Poultry gross profit plunged 48% year-on-year to $63 million in Q2 and 44% to $123 million in the first half. Adjusted EBITDA, net of IFRS 16, fell 65% year-on-year in Q2 to $30 million and 70% for the six months to $49 million, making poultry the main drag on results.

Poultry Pricing and Costs Squeeze Margins

Average poultry meat selling prices declined year-on-year in both Q2 and the first half, while sales volumes also softened. Higher production costs and a large IFRS 41 biological-assets revaluation loss, compared with a gain last year, further squeezed poultry margins.

Export Challenges in Middle East and Africa

While exports to the EU and U.K. remained largely intact, shipments to the Middle East and Africa became more difficult. These routes now take longer and cost more, reducing profitability and increasing operational complexity.

Black Sea Port Closures Disrupt Logistics

Black Sea port closures and attacks on shipping and logistics infrastructure pushed freight costs higher and disrupted loading schedules. Export reliability deteriorated, and several group logistics warehouses were destroyed, with estimated losses of about $6.5 million.

Falling Agricultural Prices and Export Limits

Since July, Ukrainian grain and oilseed prices have declined, reflecting export-capacity constraints and higher logistics costs. Management cautioned that if this trend persists, it could weigh on agriculture EBITDA in coming periods.

Agricultural Profit Likely to Reverse

Lower current grain prices are expected to trigger an adjustment to IFRS 41-related agricultural profits booked using June and July prices. As a result, management anticipates low profitability in the grain segment for the current year.

Operating Cash Flow and Working Capital Tighten

Operating cash flow in the first half fell year-on-year, hurt by lower cash earnings and weaker poultry meat prices. Working capital represented a $107 million investment, including seasonal spending on crop fields, tightening free cash generation.

CapEx Curtailed for New Ukrainian Projects

Since May 2026, MHP has completely halted new CapEx in Ukraine, reflecting heightened risk and uncertainty. Full-year CapEx is now expected at around $220 million to $240 million, focused on maintenance and projects initiated in 2025.

Logistics Costs Rise Across Segments

Management estimated about $20 million of additional logistics costs in the poultry segment alone. Vegetable oil logistics costs increased by roughly $80 per tonne, while grain exports to Europe now face similar cost burdens, eroding margins.

Short-Term Debt and Refinancing Needs

Around $150 million of debt must be repaid next year, plus about $30 million from European subsidiaries. Short-term local bank debt stands near $350 million, and the company is actively working to optimize working capital to ease refinancing pressure.

European Margins Below Long-Term Targets

UVESA’s profitability was about 8% in 2025, below MHP’s 15% long-term target. Management expects UVESA to reach double-digit margins in 2026, although not the full 15%, citing margin pressure from the collapse in Spanish pork prices.

Limited Visibility on Future Disruptions

The company stressed that the situation remains fluid, with limited visibility on the duration and ultimate impact of energy, logistics and export disruptions. This uncertainty hangs over operational planning and financial forecasts.

Guidance: Moderate EBITDA, Cost Relief Ahead

For 2026, MHP now expects EBITDA of about $420 million to $450 million, below earlier budget levels, with CapEx of around $220 million to $240 million and working-capital investment near $20 million to $30 million. Management sees gradual recovery in poultry export prices rather than a return to last year’s peaks, expects lower poultry production costs mainly from Q4 as cheaper corn and wheat feed through, and anticipates steady European price and volume trends with continued EBITDA growth; UVESA is forecast to achieve double-digit profitability in 2026 but remain short of the 15% target, while agricultural EBITDA could be weighed if low grain and oilseed prices persist.

MHP’s earnings call underscored a complex investment case: strong growth and diversification, especially in Europe and vegetable oils, but meaningful pressure on poultry margins and profitability. With refinanced debt, curtailed Ukrainian CapEx and a realistic EBITDA outlook, the group is focusing on resilience and cost efficiency as it navigates geopolitical risks and volatile commodity markets.
